title: Esna Temple's Restored Colours: Why It's Worth the Stop
excerpt: Esna Temple's cleaned ceiling: a zodiac, 46 painted vulture goddesses and red-and-yellow reliefs. What you will see, and how to add it to a Luxor to Aswan day from €67.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

Yes, Esna Temple is worth the stop. Since 2018 a joint team from Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the University of Tübingen has been lifting centuries of soot off the Temple of Khnum, revealing a zodiac ceiling, 46 painted vulture goddesses and gods in vivid red and yellow. The ceiling was finished in 2023; cleaning of some walls and columns has continued since. A visit takes about an hour, and the temple sits directly on the Luxor to Aswan road.

Use the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities monument pages to check site information and visiting details before you travel.

Most Luxor itineraries treat Esna as a coffee stop on the drive south. That advice is out of date: since 2018, restorers have been cleaning the Temple of Khnum, and the colours coming off its ceiling are worth planning an hour around. This post covers what the restoration revealed, who is doing the work, how far it has got, what a visit costs, and how Esna fits a Luxor to Aswan day. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours) is a shared-departure marketplace for Egyptian day tours and short tours, and its temple-road day tours supply the durations and prices below. We have worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

Esna Temple after restoration: the short answer

Yes, Esna Temple is worth the stop, and more so than before the restoration. Only the entrance hall of the Temple of Khnum survives, yet it preserves painted decoration in remarkable condition: the Tübingen team has called the temple's complete range of images unique in its wealth of figures and the state of preservation of its colours. The ceiling is clean, an hour is enough, and the temple sits right on the Luxor to Aswan road.

What the Esna restoration revealed

The headline find is colour. The hall spent about 1,800 years collecting soot from fires, along with dust and bird droppings; cleaning began in 2018 and the original pigments came out bright.

  • 46 vulture goddesses. The central ceiling carries 46 depictions of Nekhbet of Upper Egypt and Wadjet of Lower Egypt, both shown here as vultures with outspread wings.
  • A complete zodiac. All twelve zodiac signs, carved in two groups of six, together with Jupiter, Saturn and Mars. The ceiling is divided into seven thematic sections covering the sun's daily course, the phases of the moon, the hours of the night and New Year's Day.
  • Almost 200 new inscriptions. The cleaning brought to light almost 200 previously unknown ink inscriptions, which helped researchers identify many of the images.
  • Painted detail, 2024. The newest phase recovered paint on the clothing, crowns and thrones of the king and the Esna deities, in yellows and reds unlike Dendera's whites and light blues. The project's leader called it the greatest discovery of that year.

The French Egyptologist Serge Sauneron documented the temple systematically from the 1950s. The Tübingen team notes that the new work shows all the decorative elements in relation to one another, which a publication of the inscriptions alone could not.

Who restored Esna Temple, and is the work finished?

A joint team from Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the University of Tübingen has been restoring the temple since 2018, and the work is not entirely finished. About 30 Egyptian restorers have worked on site, and on the German side the project is led from Tübingen's Institute for Ancient Near Eastern Studies. Support has come from the Ancient Egypt Foundation, the American Research Center in Egypt and the Gerda Henkel Foundation.

Here is where it stands. By May 2022 the team had cleaned more than half the ceilings and 8 of the 18 inner columns. In October 2023 the ceiling work was announced complete, after five years. By October 2024 the southern inner wall and the southern part of the western rear wall had been cleaned, and the outer parts of the six front columns were planned for the cooler months, because the work cannot be done in summer heat. In early 2025 Archaeology magazine reported that two walls and the six front columns remained, with roughly a year and a half of work still ahead. No completion of the wall work had been announced by November 2026, and a visitor's report published in October 2026 still describes conservation as under way, with some columns cleaned and others dark with soot. You see both states in one room: bright colour beside panels still grey. Because the state of the work changes, ask your guide what is clean on the day.

What you see inside the Temple of Khnum

Only the temple's entrance hall survives, and it is one of the grandest rooms left from antiquity. The sandstone pronaos (a columned entrance vestibule) measures about 37 by 20 metres and rises about 15 metres, roofed over 24 columns, 18 inside the hall and six across the front, with varied floral capitals. Begun under Emperor Claudius (41 to 54 AD) and decorated over about 200 years, the hall also holds some of the last hieroglyphic texts ever carved, from the reign of Emperor Decius (249 to 251 AD).

Look down as well as up. Inscriptions on the hall set purity rules for worshippers, who were allowed into the temple precinct only during major festivals. The whole building sits in a pit about 9 metres below the streets of Esna, because the modern town grew up around it.

How Esna fits into a Luxor to Aswan day

Esna is about 55 to 60 km south of Luxor, an hour by road, so it is the natural first stop heading for Aswan. The Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo Temple Road tour runs the day in this order, about 8 hours in all:

  1. Luxor. Hotel pickup included.
  2. Esna. About an hour inside the Temple of Khnum, early in the day, before the heat builds.
  3. Edfu. The Temple of Horus, among the best-preserved temples in Egypt.
  4. Kom Ombo. The double temple of Sobek and Horus the Elder; lunch is included en route.
  5. Aswan. The tour ends here, so you continue south with no backtracking.

The road has routine checkpoints, so carry your passport.

The verdict on Esna Temple

Esna used to be a pass-through town; since the ceiling was cleaned it holds the most colourful ceiling between Luxor and Aswan. Give it the extra hour on the temple road. faq.a: Yes, more so than at any point in its modern history. The restored ceiling colour is the draw: a zodiac, 46 painted vulture goddesses and deities in yellow and red that survived under soot. It costs an hour and sits on the Luxor to Aswan road. The honest limits: a single hall, shared with other tour groups, and some surfaces still waiting to be cleaned.

faq.q: How much time do you need at Esna Temple?
faq.a: About an hour is enough, which is why temple-road day tours schedule exactly that. In 60 minutes you can find the zodiac signs overhead, count vulture goddesses and compare cleaned columns with sooty ones. Art lovers with sketchbooks may want two.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to visit Esna?
faq.a: October to April brings the most comfortable temperatures, and the southbound tour reaches Esna first, early in the day, before it heats up. The hall is roofed, which keeps direct sun off you, but Esna gets very hot in summer.

faq.q: Can you see Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo in one day?
faq.a: Yes, that is exactly what the temple-road tours do. Southbound from Luxor, the Esna, Edfu and Kom Ombo day takes about 8 hours and ends in Aswan, from €67 per person. Northbound from Aswan, the same three temples take about 8 hours and end in Luxor, from €60. Both prices as listed in November 2026.
